An arthropod is a type of animal. Specifically, it belongs to the largest group of animals on Earth — a group so big that it contains more than 80% of all known animal species.

To understand what makes an animal an arthropod, you need to know three core features that every arthropod shares. If an animal has all three, it's an arthropod.
The Three Defining Features

1. An exoskeleton
Unlike humans, who have bones inside our bodies, arthropods wear their skeleton on the outside. This hard outer shell, called an exoskeleton, is made of a tough material called chitin (think of it like a natural armour or a rigid suit). It protects the animal's soft inner body, gives it shape, and lets muscles attach to it from the inside.

The catch: this outer shell doesn't grow. So as the animal grows, it has to shed its old exoskeleton and grow a new, bigger one. This process is called moulting (or ecdysis). During moulting, the animal is temporarily soft and vulnerable until the new shell hardens.

2. A segmented body
An arthropod's body is not one smooth, uniform structure. It is divided into distinct segments — like a train made of connected carriages. Different groups of arthropods organise these segments differently. For example, an insect's body is grouped into three main regions: the head, the thorax (the middle section), and the abdomen (the rear section). Other arthropods may have two main body regions, or their segments may run the length of a very long body.

3. Jointed appendages
"Appendages" simply means body parts that extend outward from the body — legs, antennae, claws, pincers, mouthparts, and wings. In arthropods, all of these are jointed, meaning they have flexible hinges (like the joints in your fingers or your knee) that allow them to bend and move. This is actually the single most important thing to know: jointed limbs are what define an arthropod more than anything else.
Are Arthropods Vertebrates or Invertebrates?

Arthropods are invertebrates — they have no backbone, no spine, no internal skeleton at all. They are fundamentally different from fish, birds, reptiles, mammals, and amphibians (which are all vertebrates). Instead of bones, their support and protection comes entirely from that hard outer shell.
The Major Groups of Arthropods

Arthropoda is the name of the scientific phylum (a major category in biology) that contains all arthropods. Within this phylum, there are several major groups:

Insects
The biggest group by far. Insects have six legs, three body segments (head, thorax, abdomen), one pair of antennae, and most have wings at some life stage. Examples: ants, bees, butterflies, mosquitoes, beetles, cockroaches, dragonflies. There are over a million described species of insects alone.

Arachnids
These have eight legs, two body segments, no antennae, and no wings. Examples: spiders, scorpions, ticks, mites, and harvestmen (daddy long-legs). Arachnids are mostly land-dwelling and are found worldwide, even in extreme environments.

Crustaceans
Mostly aquatic (living in water, especially the sea), though a few live on land. They typically have ten or more legs, two pairs of antennae, and a hard, often calcified shell. Examples: crabs, lobsters, shrimp, barnacles, krill, and woodlice (the small grey creatures that curl into a ball — also called pill bugs or roly-polies, one of the few land-dwelling crustaceans).

Myriapods
The "many-legged" arthropods. There are two well-known types:

  • Centipedes: have one pair of legs per body segment, are fast-moving, and are predators (they hunt and eat other small animals). The first pair of legs is modified into venomous claws.
  • Millipedes: have two pairs of legs per body segment, are slow-moving, and feed mostly on decaying plant matter. Despite their name, they don't literally have a thousand legs, though some species come close.

Chelicerates (a broader group)
This includes arachnids (mentioned above), horseshoe crabs (ancient marine creatures that look armoured and have changed little in hundreds of millions of years), and sea spiders (small, spider-like marine animals). Chelicerates are defined by having specialised mouthpart appendages called chelicerae instead of true jaws.
Internal Biology

Despite their enormous variety, arthropods share several internal features:

  • Open circulatory system: Instead of blood flowing through a closed network of veins and arteries (like in humans), arthropod blood — called haemolymph — is pumped by a simple heart into open spaces inside the body where it washes around the organs directly, then circulates back.
  • Breathing: Different groups breathe differently. Aquatic arthropods (like crabs) use gills. Insects breathe through a network of tiny tubes called tracheae that carry air directly to their tissues. Spiders and scorpions use structures called book lungs — layered, leaf-like surfaces that extract oxygen from air.
  • Nervous system: Arthropods have a brain at the front of the body and a nerve cord that runs along the underside (the belly side) of the body, with clusters of nerve cells at each body segment.
  • Senses: Many arthropods have compound eyes — eyes made up of hundreds or thousands of tiny individual lenses, giving them a wide field of view. They also use antennae extensively for smell, touch, and even hearing.
Reproduction

Most arthropods reproduce sexually (a male and female mate). However, some species can also reproduce without mating — for example, certain insects like aphids can produce offspring from unfertilised eggs. Many arthropods lay eggs; others give birth to live young. Some, like butterflies and beetles, go through complete metamorphosis — they transform through dramatically different life stages (egg → larva → pupa → adult). Others undergo incomplete metamorphosis, where the young look like small versions of the adult from the start.
Where Do Arthropods Live?

Virtually everywhere. Arthropods have conquered every habitat on Earth:

  • Deep ocean floors and coral reefs (crabs, shrimp, krill)
  • Freshwater rivers, lakes, and ponds (water beetles, dragonfly larvae)
  • Tropical rainforests (countless insects and arachnids)
  • Deserts (scorpions, beetles)
  • The Arctic and Antarctic (cold-adapted mites and midges)
  • Inside soil (springtails, mites)
  • Inside other animals' bodies (parasitic ticks, mites, and lice)
  • High mountain altitudes
  • Even hot springs and caves
Why Arthropods Matter

Arthropods are not just plentiful — they are essential to life on Earth as we know it.

  • Pollination: Bees, butterflies, and many other insects pollinate flowering plants, making it possible for plants to reproduce and produce fruit. Without them, much of human agriculture would collapse.
  • Food chains: Arthropods are food for fish, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals. Krill alone — tiny shrimp-like crustaceans in the ocean — form the foundation of entire marine food webs, feeding whales, penguins, and fish on a massive scale.
  • Decomposition: Many arthropods (like millipedes and certain beetles and flies) break down dead plant and animal matter, recycling nutrients back into the soil.
  • Pest control: Predatory insects and spiders eat other insects that would otherwise damage crops or spread disease.
  • Disease transmission: On the negative side, some arthropods transmit serious diseases — mosquitoes spread malaria and dengue fever; ticks spread Lyme disease; fleas historically spread the bubonic plague.
  • Human food: Shrimp, crabs, lobsters, and other crustaceans are eaten by humans worldwide and form a massive global industry.
Scale and Diversity

To get a sense of how dominant arthropods are: scientists have described roughly 1.2 to 1.5 million species of arthropods, and estimates suggest there may be 5 to 10 million total species (most undiscovered, particularly insects in tropical regions). Compare that to mammals (about 6,500 species) or birds (about 10,000 species). In terms of total biomass — the combined weight of all individuals — insects alone outweigh all wild land vertebrates combined.

In terms of size, arthropods range from the microscopic (certain parasitic mites are less than 0.1 mm long) to the impressively large: the Japanese spider crab can have a leg span of up to 3.7 metres (12 feet). The coconut crab, the largest land-dwelling arthropod, can weigh up to 4 kg (9 pounds).
In Summary

An arthropod is an invertebrate animal with three defining traits: a hard exoskeleton on the outside, a segmented body, and jointed appendages. The major groups include insects, arachnids, crustaceans, and myriapods. Arthropods are the most diverse, numerous, and widespread animals on Earth, occupying every habitat and playing irreplaceable roles in ecosystems. They are ancient — the arthropod body plan has existed for over 500 million years — and extraordinarily successful by every biological measure.
